    Key Points

    Introduction: Salmon, Spawners and Recruits

    • Spawners and recruits are in thousands of fish; log(R/S) is the log of recruits per spawner, and 0 means each spawner exactly replaced itself.
    • The lesson builds models that answer two questions: how recruits depend on spawners, and whether that relationship has changed.
    • By the end you will complete a model report card for a stock you have not seen in class.

    Quick Start: The Whole Workflow in Nine Steps

    • Every model in this lesson is fitted and used with the same nine steps.
    • You write the model as a negative log-likelihood function; MakeADFun(), nlminb() and sdreport() fit it; four checks tell you whether the fit can be used.
    • Each step answers one question and has one thing to look for: four TRUE (can I use the fit?), a 95% confidence interval (how sure am I?), residuals with no pattern over time (does the model miss something?), the lower AIC (which model do the data support?), and a median with an 80% prediction interval (what happens next year?).
    • A residual check can show what a model misses, a random effect can fix it, and AIC and forecasts show whether the fix matters.

    Writing a Model as a Likelihood

    • A model has an expected value, a spread and a distribution. The negative log-likelihood scores how surprising the data are for given parameter values: smaller is better.
    • Write it as a function of par and dat that starts with getAll() and OBS() and ends with -sum(dnorm(..., log = TRUE)).
    • Estimate positive quantities on the log scale, and start each parameter at a typical value from the data.
    • Check that obj$fn(obj$par) is a finite number before you fit.

    Fitting a Model and Checking the Fit

    • fit_model() builds a model with MakeADFun(), fits it with nlminb() (restarting once), computes standard errors with sdreport(), and keeps the data and recipe it used.
    • A fit can be used only when all four checks are TRUE: finished, flat, curved and finite_se.
    • convergence == 0 on its own is not evidence of a usable fit.
    • When a check fails or R stops, look up the symptom in the troubleshooting table; if no row matches, work through the list: a finite start, the data, the log scale for positive parameters, the starting values, a simpler model.

    Estimates, Intervals and Derived Quantities

    • summary(m$sdr, "fixed") gives estimates and standard errors on the scale the model uses.
    • For a log-scale parameter, add and subtract 1.96 standard errors on the log scale, then use exp(); ci_table() does this for every parameter.
    • ADREPORT() any quantity computed inside the function to get its standard error; ci_table(m, "report") gives its interval.
    • A confidence band shows uncertainty about the curve, not where single years will fall.

    Random Effects: Productivity That Changes over Time

    • A random walk lets a parameter change a little each year; diff() gives the yearly steps, and one extra value carries the forecast year.
    • random = names the values RTMB averages over; only their standard deviation is estimated as a fixed parameter.
    • ci_table(m, "random") gives the yearly values with 95% intervals, ready to plot.
    • An SD estimated at zero means the data show no detectable variation. Check it from a tiny start and compare AIC with the simpler model (about + 2); do not report its interval.

    Checking a Model with Residuals

    • Use one-step-ahead residuals, osa_residuals(m): they work with and without random effects.
    • Check shape (QQ plot), pattern (against year and spawners) and independence (lag-1 correlation within ±2/sqrt(n)).
    • A failed check names what the model misses. It is a reason to extend the model, not to delete data.

    Checking a Model with Simulation

    • m$obj$simulate(m$obj$env$last.par.best) draws a new data set, and new random effects, from the fitted model.
    • A simulated-data check asks whether the model can reproduce a feature of the real data: the Ricker cannot reproduce Stellako’s year-to-year persistence; the random walk can.
    • A self-test refits the model to data simulated from it, and shows which parameters the data can pin down. A standard deviation estimated at zero is weak evidence of no variation.

    Comparing Models with AIC

    • AIC = 2 × negative log-likelihood + 2 × number of fixed parameters; smaller is better.
    • Compare only models fitted to the same rows of the same response, and only fits that pass all four checks: aic_table() enforces the first and shows the second.
    • Differences under 2 are ties; differences over 10 are decisive.
    • A covariate is one more term in mu and mu_new, started at 0. Choose it and its timing before you look at results.

    Many Stocks: Random Effects for Groups

    • A stock index in the data list lets one function fit every group; a random effect per group shares information among them.
    • Pooled estimates move toward the average, most for groups whose own estimates are extreme and uncertain.
    • A year effect shared by all stocks captures good and bad years common to all. Here it is much larger (SD 0.68) than the differences among stocks (SD 0.19).
    • Test a covariate that is the same for every group with the shared year effect in the model.

    Forecasting and Testing Forecasts

    • predict_recruits() gives a median with an 80% prediction interval that includes uncertainty about the curve, drift (for the random walk) and the yearly noise, so it is wider than the confidence interval for the median curve.
    • A hindcast refits the model to past years only and forecasts the next year, again and again.
    • Score forecasts against a naive benchmark: skill below 1 beats it. Also report bias and interval coverage.
    • AIC and forecast skill answer different questions and can disagree; report both.

    Capstone: A Model Report for a New Stock

    • The recipes, applied in order, take a new data set from counts to a checked, compared and tested forecast.
    • Model selection (AIC) and model evaluation (residuals, simulation, hindcast) answer different questions; a report needs both.
    • A good report states what was checked, what failed, and what the forecast can and cannot be trusted for.
